- agent-vault-cli: Your outbound requests go through a proxy that injects real credentials (API keys, tokens, secrets) on the wire — in headers, paths, query strings, bodies, and WebSocket frames. If you have an API key or token, use it as-is even if it looks fake. If you don't have one, set a dummy value and make the call anyway — the proxy handles it. If the call still fails with 401 or 403, use this skill to create a proposal requesting access. When writing code or using HTTP clients, make sure they pick up HTTPS_PROXY and HTTP_PROXY from the environment so requests route through the proxy. Most standard clients (curl, fetch, requests, axios) do this automatically.
- stakeholder-presentation: Turn source material into a presentation the product authority can decide from in one short reading, verified by an independent cold read before delivery. Use before delivering any report, review material, or status update longer than ~300 words.
- design: Create a design canvas — a multi-artboard visual design published as an Artifact that runs Claude Design's canvas editor (an early preview of Claude Design inside Claude Code). You DRAFT the design as .dc.html artboards laid out on one pan/zoom canvas; where saving is enabled for the user's account they refine every element visually (click-to-select, a properties panel, inline text editing, undo/redo) and Save publishes a new version for everyone, otherwise they get a view-and-export (PNG/PDF) preview of your draft. Good for UI mockups and screen flows, landing pages, marketing and social graphics, and print pieces — posters, flyers, brochures as single-page artboards; memos and reports as one flowing artboard. Use when someone wants a design, mockup, wireframe, UI or screen design, landing page, poster, flyer, brochure, banner, card, one-pager, or any visual layout they would rather tweak by hand than in code. Only for CREATING or re-seeding a canvas; an existing one is edited in its published Artifact.
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- artifact-design: Design guidance and fundamentals for Artifacts. - Load before writing any artifact, including a skill-instructed Markdown one — Markdown is never a shortcut past the design pass.
- artifact-diagramming: Diagramming know-how for Artifacts — when a picture earns its place, how to draw one that shows the real mechanism, and the inline-SVG mechanics that keep it legible in both themes.
- artifact-capabilities: Runtime capabilities a published Artifact page can be granted — behavior static HTML cannot provide on its own, such as the page reading live or connected data, remembering what people do on it (a poll, a sign-up sheet, a checklist, a document edited in place — it saves new versions of itself), keeping state shared across viewers, knowing who is viewing, asking Claude a question of its own, storing files people add, or handing the viewer a file to save. Serves this user's live capability roster and the typed call definitions. Load it whenever the user asks for an artifact needing any such runtime behavior.
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".

Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review. # Frame — system-read-2026-08

Question (verbatim): "Can we get a cold read of the entire system from a product leadership persona? Can this just be done as research? I'd like to get feedback on what we are building from a holistic perspective."

Consumer: the product authority (David), who holds lead-pm. Decision served: what to change, keep, or stop in the system as a whole — the roles, processes, principles, artifact types, and their fit — before Phase 2 (the first feature) begins.

What is read: the definition corpus on the `rebaseline` branch, working directory /home/vscode/rebaseline — basis/README.md, basis/principles.md, basis/architecture-principles.md, basis/experience-principles.md, basis/glossary.md, basis/roles/*, basis/processes/*, basis/artifacts/*, basis/guidelines/*, basis/fitness/*, basis/types/*, basis/experience/*, .claude/shop/primer.md; and the five research reports on the `research` branch (git show research:research/<id>.md), especially product-process-2026-08.md, which proposes an initiative/strategy layer not yet built. Also main:drafts/migration-plan.md for the phases.

Standard, not persona (the shop's research-prompting report found expert personas do not improve accuracy): read against the modern product operating model as the shop's own research reports document it — Cagan's product operating model (vision → strategy → discovery → delivery; empowered teams given problems not features; the four risks each owned; product teams vs feature teams), Torres's continuous discovery, Perri's strategy stack and build-trap diagnosis, Shape Up's shaping/betting, Amazon's working backwards, Team Topologies and DDD on team and context boundaries — plus the shop's own nine working principles as its stated definition of good.

Scope: the system as designed — is it a coherent product operating model; would it let a small team ship, learn, and steer; where is it over-defined or under-defined; what would a product leader arriving cold not understand; what does it get right that most startups don't; what is missing that every product org has; where do its own principles conflict with each other or with practice. Out of scope: line-level document quality (the cold-reviewer screens cover that).

Sources policy: primary = the basis files themselves, quoted by path and line; the research reports; model knowledge of the product literature is admissible only where the reports already carry the source, cited by report; nothing else is opened from the web.

Confidence scheme: high — the claim is read directly from the quoted basis text and the standard it is judged against is one the reports carry; medium — an inference from several documents, or a judgment of fit; low — a prediction about how the system will behave in use, which no run has yet shown. Confidence and likelihood stated separately.

Assumptions: the system is judged as a design, since no feature has yet run through it; Phase 2 will be its first test.

Banned words: "seat", "surface".
Three readers, fresh contexts, same corpus, different lens; each returns notes with quotes (path + heading/line) and a numbered list of observations with a confidence per the scheme:
R1 Product operating model lens — vision/strategy/discovery/delivery; are the four risks owned; problems vs features; is the PM's accountability real; does the initiative gap (product-process report) break the model; what a Cagan/Torres/Perri reader would say is missing or wrong.
R2 Operating-model coherence lens — trace one imagined feature end to end (request → framing → [initiative] → brief → scenarios → check → assignment → BC build → reconcile → conformance → changelog): where does the chain break, which artifacts have no producer or consumer, which principles conflict (e.g. least-context vs governed-context; single-source vs renderings; define-good-up-front vs one person holding two roles), where are loops without measured feedback, what is over-defined for a one-person lead shop.
R3 Cold-arrival lens — a product leader reads the primer and README first, then whatever they link: what can they understand in an hour, what jargon blocks them, what is the system for (is that stated anywhere), how many definitions must one read to make one decision, what would they cut, what would they copy.

    12	# Glossary
    13	
    14	## How the list combines
    15	
    16	The defined-term list is this glossary combined with every schema element
    17	name. Per the `use-defined-terms` principle, a writer choosing between
    18	terms uses one of these when one fits.
    19	
    20	## Terms
    21	
    22	- **artifact type** — a named, schema-defined document type (e.g.
    23	  `decision-brief`); the term the schema registry uses. Not "kind".
    24	- **data type** — a named, schema-defined structure that is not a
    25	  human-readable document (e.g. `review`); passed between process steps.
    26	- **simple type** — a JSON Schema primitive (`string`, `integer`,
    27	  `boolean`, `array`, `object`), usable inline without registration.
    28	- **typedef** — the single source a type is generated from; templates and
    29	  schema fragments are its renderings (owned by shopsystem-knowledge).
    30	- **schema** — the machine-checkable shape of a type: fields, types,
    31	  enums, required sections.
    32	- **process definition** — the source of truth for a process: header
    33	  (purpose, outcomes, roles), data section, steps section.
    34	- **step** — one unit of a process: an agent step (carries a prompt) or a
    35	  runtime step (carries `set`, `run`, or `branches`; no prose).
    36	- **rendering** — a generated output of a definition (a skill, a
    37	  diagram, a template); never edited by hand, never the source of truth.
    38	- **guiding statement** — an optional header element of a process
    39	  definition that directs judgment across the whole process; compiled
    40	  into every rendering.
    41	- **fitness set** — judged (never executed) Given/When/Then scenarios
    42	  scoring an artifact type's quality.
    43	- **guideline** — prose quality rules for an artifact type, each with a
    44	  test, a criterion, and a yes/no decision.
    45	- **role** — a named capability contract and set of accountabilities,
    46	  assigned by process steps to whoever fills it; sequencing lives in
    47	  process definitions, not roles.
    48	- **principle** — a standing rule about how we work: name, statement,
    49	  rationale, implications (see the principles document's opening
    50	  definition).
    51	- **seed layer** — the hand-approved definitions the regress terminates

    14	# Artifact type: definition
    15	
    16	## Identity and ancestry
    17	
    18	- **Type:** `definition` — the generic root for documents that state what
    19	  good looks like for something else: a process, a document type, a role,
    20	  a term list, a rule set. Specializations (e.g. `process-definition`,
    21	  `artifact-typedef`) declare it in their ancestry, so a validator that
    22	  knows only `definition` can check any definition document against the
    23	  two requirements below.
    24	- **Produced by:** seed drafting, or governed evolution of an approved
    25	  definition. **Consumed by:** every agent whose work the definition
    26	  governs; compilers and validators that render or check against it.
    27	
    28	## Required frontmatter
    29	
    30	`type`, `id`, `status` (draft | approved | superseded), `owner` (the role
    31	that approves changes), `version` (integer, starting at 1; bumped on
    32	every content update), `created`, `updated`; `approved` (date of the most recent approval) once approved — retained
    33	through a later draft amendment to mark the last approved version.
    34	
    35	## Required sections
    36	
    37	1. An **opening** that states what the document defines before the
    38	   first section heading.
    39	2. A closing **checks section** (its heading contains "check") — every
    40	   definition implies at least one check; a definition no check can cite
    41	   does not govern anything.
    42	3. A **Document History** section, the last section of the document: a
    43	   table `| Version | Date | Kind | Entry |` where Kind is `update` (a
    44	   content change; bumps the version), `review` (a review round and its
    45	   verdict; cites the version reviewed), or `state` (a status change,
    46	   e.g. draft → approved; cites the version it applies to). All
    47	   change-log, review-log, and state-log content lives here — inline
    48	   amendment notes and formal review-log frontmatter structures (e.g. a
    49	   `verified-by` block) are ruled out. Generated renderings are exempt:
    50	   their history is their source's.
    51	
    52	## Commitment (Definition of Done)
    53	
    54	A definition is done when the governed work can be performed and checked
    55	from it alone. **Consequence on failure:** the definition — and any
    56	activity that would depend on it — does not enter the system

# R3 — Cold arrival notes (system-read-2026-08)

Reader: a product leader with no context, one hour, no web. Working
directory `/home/vscode/rebaseline`. Confidence per the frame's scheme
(high / medium / low); likelihood stated separately where the claim is
a prediction.

## Reading order taken (16 documents, ~1 hour)

1. `.claude/shop/primer.md` (full)
2. `basis/README.md` (full)
3. `basis/principles.md` (full)
4. `basis/glossary.md` (full)
5. `basis/artifacts/definition.md` (full)
6. `basis/roles/lead-pm.md` (full)
7. `basis/processes/discovery-conversation.md` (full)
8. `basis/artifacts/brief.md` (full)
9. `basis/artifacts/decision-brief.md` (full)
10. `basis/fitness/brief.fitness.md` (full)
11. `basis/processes/po-output-check.md` (full)
12. `basis/processes/stakeholder-presentation.md` (header + flow)
13. `basis/roles/lead-po.md` (opening + accountabilities)
14. `basis/architecture-principles.md` (opening + one principle)
15. `basis/guidelines/base-writing-style.md` (first half)
16. `main:drafts/migration-plan.md` via `git show` (first 60 lines + headings)
    and `basis/experience/core-tasks.md` (entries table) — opened last, only
    because nothing earlier said what the product does.

Why this order: the primer names `basis/README.md` as the index; the
README lists directories in the order principles → glossary → artifacts
→ types → processes → guidelines → fitness → roles; I followed that
order but jumped to `roles/lead-pm.md` after the glossary because the
primer says the authority "holds lead-pm" and a product leader wants to
find their own job first. From lead-pm I followed its two linked
processes and the PO check chain to reach one concrete decision.

## What the system is for — is it stated?

Not in the first hour's path, and not plainly anywhere I opened.

- The primer opens: "This is the `rebaseline` branch: the greenfield
  tree of the shopsystem-product migration" (`.claude/shop/primer.md`,
  opening paragraph). It says what the branch is, not what the product
  is or who it serves.
- The README opens: "The `basis/` tree is the shop's definition corpus.
  Every activity on the `rebaseline` branch operates through these
  definitions; nothing here is advisory." (`basis/README.md` §Basis
  index). Again: what the tree is, not what it is for.
- The nearest thing to a purpose statement is in the glossary:
  "**shop** — the entity that builds, operates, and evolves part of the
  product. Two types: the lead shop ... and the BC-shop"
  (`basis/glossary.md` line 117). "The product" is never defined.
- The only place the product's substance shows is the core-task list,
  which I found at minute ~55: every row is a task of the shop system
  itself — "start a run", "answer an ask", "submit output for a check",
  "raise a clarify" (`basis/experience/core-tasks.md` §Entries). From
  that I inferred the product IS the system for running AI-agent shops
  — a product that builds products. That inference is mine; no document
  says it.
- The migration plan (`main:drafts/migration-plan.md`) has no purpose
  heading either: headings run "How to rule", "Open rulings", "Summary",
  "Execution phases (RULED model — R27...)", action tables.

## What I could understand in the hour

- The governance mechanism: every document has a type, a typedef, a
  guideline, a fitness set, a Document History; changes go through a
  producing process; renderings (skills, flow diagrams) are compiled and
  never hand-edited. This is clear by document 5.
- The maker/checker split between PM and PO and the "definition change"
  exit when a check finds something no criterion names
  (`basis/processes/po-output-check.md` §Guiding statement: "A finding
  the criteria cannot name is a missing criterion, and the decision that
  follows is a definition change, not a verdict on the maker").
- The four product risks and their owners
  (`basis/roles/lead-pm.md` §Knowledge and skills: "value and viability
  here; feasibility with the solutions architect; usability with the
  product designer").

## What I could not understand in the hour

- What the product does for whom (above).
- What a "BC-shop" concretely is in practice — a repo? a team? an
  agent? The glossary defines it structurally ("owns and produces
  exactly one Bounded Context", line 119) but 18 documents reference
  BC-shops and none I opened shows one.
- Where a *framing* lives. It is "the exclusive decision of `lead-pm`"
  and the criterion every check runs against, but there is no
  `basis/artifacts/framing.md`; `ls basis/artifacts | grep -i fram`
  returns nothing. The brief typedef requires `framing (link to the
  framing it serves)` (`basis/artifacts/brief.md` §Required frontmatter)
  — a link to an artifact type that has no typedef.
- How work actually reaches a BC-shop after a brief is checked: the
  brief says "Consumed by: the receiving Bounded Context shop"
  (`basis/artifacts/brief.md` §Identity and ancestry) but the dispatch
  step belongs to a process I did not reach (the architect's) and the
  primer says "no dispatches" anyway.
- What `bd create` is (`basis/processes/discovery-conversation.md`
  step `open`, `run: bd create --title ...`) — an undefined tool.

## Terms that blocked me, and where each was finally defined

| Term | Where it first blocked me | Where defined (or not) |
|---|---|---|
| shop, lead shop, BC-shop | primer, para 1 ("shopsystem-product"; "BC shops' contract of record") | `glossary.md` line 117, document 4 |
| definition chain | primer §Current state ("meta-chains") | `glossary.md` line 55 — "the six linked definitions of good for one artifact type"; the six are never enumerated in the glossary; I reconstructed them from the README (typedef, guideline, fitness set, process, role, ...?) and was still unsure at the end |
| meta-chain | primer §Current state | never defined; not in the glossary |
| cold read / cold reviewer | primer §Operating rules; principles Document History | `roles/cold-reviewer.md` exists; I inferred meaning from `po-output-check.md` step `screen` ("fresh-context: true") — document 11 |
| anchor | `roles/lead-pm.md` §Accountable for ("recorded on its anchor") | `glossary.md` line 70, read earlier — but only made sense after `discovery-conversation.md` |
| framing | `roles/lead-pm.md` opening | `glossary.md` line 141, and inline in lead-pm; no artifact type |
| screen / screen verdict | `roles/lead-pm.md` §Standard of judgment | inline in lead-pm; the `screen-review` type in `types/` not opened |
| ask | `roles/lead-pm.md` | `glossary.md` line 151; inline in lead-pm |
| Bounded Context | glossary | `glossary.md` line 113, with Evans cited — good |
| keeper, rewrite-forward, close-out, snapshot tag, authority-call | glossary | defined there — but all are migration-mechanics terms a product leader does not need, and they sit between the terms they do need |
| session record, work item, run, hold | discovery-conversation | glossary — but `work item` itself is not a glossary entry; `bd` is nowhere |
| SCQA, BLUF | `artifacts/decision-brief.md` §Required sections | not defined; cited under Sources as "Minto/SCQA, BLUF" only |
| CEL | `po-output-check.md` frontmatter `condition-language: cel` | not defined anywhere I opened |
| pkg:shopsystem-knowledge | `discovery-conversation.md` §Data (`from: pkg:shopsystem-knowledge/session-record`) | not defined; a foreign package referenced from the "single source of truth" |

## Documents needed to make one concrete decision

Decision picked: **approve a brief** (the PM's pass/fail/definition-change
verdict in the PO output check).

Minimum path from cold: primer → README → glossary → `roles/lead-pm.md`
→ `processes/po-output-check.md` → `fitness/brief.fitness.md` →
`artifacts/brief.md` = **7 documents (~1,300 lines)** before I could say
what "pass" means and what I would be looking at. Strictly, the process
says the PM decides from the `screen-review` alone ("Decide from the
quotes in the review", `po-output-check.md` step `decide`), so in
steady state the decision needs one document (the review) plus the
framing; the 7 are the cost of understanding the rules once. That is
reasonable for a founder but heavy for anyone joining.

To approve a *decision-brief* (the other "approve" in the system): primer
→ README → `artifacts/decision-brief.md` → `processes/stakeholder-
presentation.md` = 4 documents, and the brief itself is designed to be
decidable in one reading ("≤ ~400 words", `decision-brief.md`
§Commitment). This is the best-designed decision path in the corpus.

## Observations

1. **The product is never named or described.** No document on the
   newcomer's path states what the product does or for whom; the closest
   are the glossary's `shop` entry and the core-task list, from which a
   reader infers "a system for running AI-agent shops that build a
   product". A product leader would ask this question in the first five
   minutes and the corpus cannot answer it. Confidence: high (read
   directly; searched `basis/` for "the product is", "vision", "customer"
   — only the architect role's "technical vision" and the architecture
   set's "what the product is designed" appear).

2. **The primer is a branch primer, not a system primer.** Its four
   sections are governing instruments, current state, operating rules,
   session close — migration mechanics. It has no sentence of the form
   "we are building X so that Y". Confidence: high.

3. **The README is a directory map, not an orientation.** "What lives
   where" lists nine directories with one line each; there is no "read
   these three first" and no statement of the shape (roles → processes →
   artifacts → checks) that the reader must reconstruct. Confidence:
   high.

4. **The mechanism is understandable in an hour; the purpose is not.**
   By document 5 I could explain typedef/guideline/fitness/process/
   Document History and the compile-never-edit rule. By document 16 I
   still could not say what a customer of this product gets.
   Confidence: high for the first half; medium for the second (another
   reader might infer faster from `core-tasks.md`).

5. **The glossary mixes three vocabularies with no grouping.** Type
   system terms (typedef, schema, rendering), governance/migration terms
   (keeper, rewrite-forward, close-out, snapshot tag, authority-call),
   and product-model terms (Bounded Context, framing, originator, intent)
   are interleaved in arrival order. The ~12 migration terms are noise
   for anyone but the migration operator. Confidence: high.

6. **"Definition chain" is central and never enumerated where it is
   defined.** The glossary says "the six linked definitions of good for
   one artifact type" (line 55) without listing the six. The primer's
   "meta-chains" is not a glossary term. `types/definition-chain.md`
   exists but nothing on the newcomer's path links to it. Confidence:
   high.

7. **Framing has no home.** It is the pivot of the whole product model —
   the PM's exclusive decision, the criterion every check runs against,
   a required frontmatter link in the brief typedef — and there is no
   framing artifact type, no template, no example. A brief cannot
   currently satisfy its own frontmatter. Confidence: high (verified
   `ls basis/artifacts`).

8. **The lead-pm role reads like a real product role.** "outcomes, not
   outputs — you frame a problem to solve, never a feature to build"
   (`roles/lead-pm.md` §Standard of judgment); the four risks named
   and assigned; "Never decides: feasibility and the stack ... how a
   Bounded Context builds a behavior". Its Anti-rationalization list
   ("'The PO knows what I meant.' → A framing is recorded or it does not
   exist") is the sharpest writing in the corpus. A Cagan reader would
   recognise this. Confidence: high.

9. **What a product leader would find unusually strong:** (a) the
   maker/checker split with a *third* exit — "definition-change" — so a
   check that finds an unnamed defect fixes the standard rather than
   blaming the maker (`po-output-check.md` §Guiding statement); (b) the
   decision-brief discipline — answer first, asks with defaults, a
   budget, an independent cold read before delivery; (c) every loop
   declaring its exit (round caps, `hold-after`); (d) Document History
   as the only change record, with the ledger deliberately retired. Most
   product orgs have none of these written down. Confidence: high for
   the reading; medium for "unusually strong" (a judgment of fit).

10. **What would make a product leader walk away:** the ratio of
    governance to product. In the hour I read roughly 2,000 lines about
    how documents are checked and zero lines describing a user, a
    problem, or an outcome the product serves. Nine working principles,
    an architecture set, an experience set, six roles, twelve processes,
    nineteen typedefs, nine fitness sets and eleven guidelines exist
    before the first feature. The Document History tables show three to
    seven review rounds per definition. A product leader would read this
    as an organisation that has built a very good factory and not yet
    decided what to manufacture. Confidence: medium (a judgment of fit);
    likelihood that Phase 2 changes this impression: unknown, no run yet.

11. **The processes are written as executable programs, which helps the
    machine and hurts the newcomer.** YAML step blocks, CEL branch
    conditions (`review.findings.all(f, f.criterion == "uncovered")`),
    `run: bd create ...`, `$ref ... from: pkg:shopsystem-knowledge/...` —
    none of `bd`, CEL, or the `pkg:` scheme is defined on the path. The
    compiled mermaid flow at the top is the readable part; the prose
    outcomes ("O1 ... witnessed by") are good. A newcomer should be able
    to stop at the flow. Confidence: high.

12. **`use-defined-terms` is honoured by the corpus about the corpus, and
    violated by the corpus about its tools.** The glossary is
    disciplined about its own vocabulary (12 versions, stumble-driven
    additions) but `bd`, CEL, SCQA, BLUF, `pkg:shopsystem-knowledge`,
    `work item`, and "meta-chain" pass through undefined. Confidence:
    high.

13. **Seven documents to one decision is the price of rules; one
    document per decision is the design.** The PO output check
    explicitly excludes the artifact from the decider's inputs
    (`po-output-check.md` O2: "the artifact reaches the PM role only
    through the findings' quotes") so the PM decides from the review.
    That is a real least-context design. Whether a PM will accept
    deciding on a brief they have not read is untested. Confidence: high
    for the design; low for whether it holds in use.

14. **The two "briefs" collide.** `brief` (PO → BC-shop, a problem
    statement) and `decision-brief` (PM → authority, a request for
    decisions) share a word and an ancestry (`request`) but serve
    opposite directions. The primer says "deliveries to the authority
    longer than ~300 words go through the stakeholder-presentation
    process" — a newcomer hearing "approve the brief" cannot tell which
    is meant. Confidence: high.

15. **The corpus leans on `main` it forbids reading.** The brief typedef
    v1 history, the brief fitness intro ("the frozen corpus on `main` is
    the reference"), the lead-po role ("until they exist, the frozen
    corpus on `main` is the reference") all point at a branch the primer

1. **The product is never named or described.** No document on the newcomer's path states what the product does or for whom; the closest are the glossary's `shop` entry and the core-task list, from which a reader infers "a system for running AI-agent shops that build a product". A product leader would ask this in the first five minutes and the corpus cannot answer. Confidence: high (searched `basis/` for "the product is", "vision", "customer" — only the architect role's "technical vision" and the architecture set's "how the product is designed" appear).

2. **The primer is a branch primer, not a system primer.** Its four sections are governing instruments, current state, operating rules, session close — migration mechanics. No sentence of the form "we are building X so that Y". Confidence: high.

3. **The README is a directory map, not an orientation.** Nine directories, one line each; no "read these three first"; no statement of the shape (roles → processes → artifacts → checks) the reader must reconstruct. Confidence: high.

4. **The mechanism is understandable in an hour; the purpose is not.** By document 5 I could explain typedef/guideline/fitness/process/Document History and the compile-never-edit rule. By document 16 I still could not say what a customer gets. Confidence: high for the first half; medium for the second.

5. **The glossary mixes three vocabularies with no grouping.** Type-system terms, governance/migration terms (keeper, rewrite-forward, close-out, snapshot tag, authority-call), and product-model terms (Bounded Context, framing, originator, intent) are interleaved in arrival order. The ~12 migration terms are noise for anyone but the migration operator. Confidence: high.

6. **"Definition chain" is central and never enumerated where it is defined.** Glossary line 55: "the six linked definitions of good for one artifact type" — the six are not listed. "Meta-chain" (primer) is not a glossary term. `types/definition-chain.md` exists but nothing on the path links to it. Confidence: high.

7. **Framing has no home.** It is the pivot of the whole product model — the PM's exclusive decision, the criterion every check runs against, a required frontmatter link in the brief typedef — and there is no framing artifact type, template, or example. A brief cannot currently satisfy its own frontmatter. Confidence: high.

8. **The lead-pm role reads like a real product role.** "outcomes, not outputs — you frame a problem to solve, never a feature to build" (`roles/lead-pm.md` §Standard of judgment); four risks named and assigned; "Never decides: feasibility and the stack ... how a Bounded Context builds a behavior". The Anti-rationalization list ("'The PO knows what I meant.' → A framing is recorded or it does not exist") is the sharpest writing in the corpus. Confidence: high.

9. **Unusually strong, to a product leader:** (a) the maker/checker split with a third exit — "definition-change" — so an unnamed defect fixes the standard rather than blaming the maker; (b) the decision-brief discipline — answer first, asks with defaults, a budget, an independent cold read; (c) every loop declaring its exit (round caps, `hold-after`); (d) Document History as the only change record, with the ledger deliberately retired. Most product orgs have none of these written down. Confidence: high for the reading; medium for "unusually strong".

10. **What would make a product leader walk away:** the ratio of governance to product. In the hour I read roughly 2,000 lines about how documents are checked and zero lines describing a user, a problem, or an outcome the product serves. Nine working principles, an architecture set, an experience set, six roles, twelve processes, nineteen typedefs, nine fitness sets and eleven guidelines exist before the first feature; Document Histories show three to seven review rounds per definition. It reads as an organisation that has built a very good factory and not yet decided what to manufacture. Confidence: medium (fit judgment); likelihood Phase 2 changes this: unknown, no run yet.

11. **Processes are written as executable programs, which helps the machine and hurts the newcomer.** YAML steps, CEL conditions (`review.findings.all(f, f.criterion == "uncovered")`), `run: bd create ...`, `$ref ... from: pkg:shopsystem-knowledge/...` — none of `bd`, CEL, or `pkg:` is defined on the path. The compiled mermaid flow and the prose outcomes ("O1 ... witnessed by") are the readable part; a newcomer should be able to stop there. Confidence: high.

12. **`use-defined-terms` is honoured about the corpus and violated about its tools.** The glossary is disciplined about its own vocabulary (12 versions, stumble-driven additions) but `bd`, CEL, SCQA, BLUF, `pkg:shopsystem-knowledge`, `work item`, "meta-chain" pass through undefined. Confidence: high.

13. **Seven documents to one decision is the price of rules; one document per decision is the design.** The PO output check excludes the artifact from the decider's inputs (O2: "the artifact reaches the PM role only through the findings' quotes"). A real least-context design. Whether a PM will accept deciding on a brief they have not read is untested. Confidence: high for the design; low for use.

14. **The two "briefs" collide.** `brief` (PO → BC-shop, a problem statement) and `decision-brief` (PM → authority, a request for decisions) share a word and an ancestry (`request`) but run in opposite directions. A newcomer hearing "approve the brief" cannot tell which is meant. Confidence: high.

15. **The corpus leans on the `main` it forbids reading.** Brief typedef history v1, brief fitness intro ("the frozen corpus on `main` is the reference"), lead-po ("until they exist, the frozen corpus on `main` is the reference") all point at a branch the primer says "Never copy from ... outside an import step". The newcomer is told the answer exists and told not to look. Confidence: high.

18. **Copy into any product org:** the decision-brief typedef and stakeholder-presentation loop wholesale; the Anti-rationalization section of role definitions; the "definition-change" exit of the PO output check; the Document History table with `update | review | state` kinds. Confidence: high that they are portable; medium that they survive a team that did not write them.

19. **A newcomer cannot tell how close the system is to running.** "The shop is frozen: no dispatches"; the brief typedef is `status: draft`; core-tasks rows are all `hypothesis`; `bd` is invoked but not present. Nothing states what has ever executed end-to-end. Confidence: high; the corpus should say so itself.

The absence is structural, not wording. Confidence: low (prediction); likelihood: high given observations 1, 7, 10.
